messages.author: c052ac5727650828
messages.subject: problem with implementing Spike and Slab prior for logistic regression
parts:
Dear Stan community,

I am new to STAN and sampling approach. I would like to use STAN to play with different modeling assumptions for my problem and I think STAN is such a good choice because it allows to check my assumptions without worrying about re-deriving varational update. 

As a start, I would like to implement "spike and slab" prior for logistic regression (which I can extend for the rest of my model if it works):

the spike and slab is as follows:

y           {0,1 }    <--- observed variable
gamma[m]  ~ Bernoulli(theta[m])      // selector variable
w[m]    ~  Normal(mu[m],sigma[m])   // coefficient
beta[m]   =  gamma[m]*w[m]
y[n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(x[n] * beta)); 

M is number of features and N is number of samples. I have included my implementation. To generate data for testing, I used the the R script in 

[STANHOME]/src/models/speed/logistic/logistic_generate_data.R

an example data is also attached. 

However, it does not look like that  my model is working. When I check the "sample.csv" file, many of the parameters are all zero !? For example, check the "sample.csv" file and values of the gammas and betas, could some one please explain this? am I missing something.


Thanks,
Kayhan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] problem with implementing Spike and Slab prior for logistic regression
parts: hopefully an expert will reply to you, but the obvious thing that might improve numerical stability would be to replace bernoulli(inv_logit()) with bernoulli_logit().  i also wonder if your data requires a more informative prior on theta[m] to enforce sparsity, depending on the size of M relative to N.

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] problem with implementing Spike and Slab prior for logistic regression
parts:
Hi Kayhan,

At present there is no way to implement spike-and-slab priors in Stan,
because they involve discrete latent variables which cannot be sampled
using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo/NUTS. A later release will include
support for Gibbs sampling for latent discrete variables, but it's not
available right now.

If you don't have many predictors, you might consider summing over all
of the possible settings of gamma, but it'll be quite expensive even
for m in the single digits. Unfortunately, this is one of the few
kinds of models that there aren't really good tricks for sampling in
Stan.

Note also that these models can be painfully slow to mix even with a
well tuned custom sampler. In general, sampling from spike-and-slab
posteriors is tantamount to solving an intractable combinatorial
optimization problem. (Which is why the L1 convex relaxation of the
spike penalty is so popular in the point estimation literature.)

Matt

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] problem with implementing Spike and Slab prior for logistic regression
parts:
Hi Kayhan,

No, people often have reasonable success with Gibbs samplers. Usually
the results are no worse than those obtained using variational
inference (although, as usual when comparing MCMC and variational
approaches, Gibbs may take longer). However, it seems as though these
samplers work poorly when it's not possible to integrate out either
the continuous or the discrete parameters, since there are such strong
posterior dependencies between them. For a (non-conjugate) logistic
regression, integrating out the regression coefficients isn't an
option, but you might be able to adapt the approach of Wang&Blei
(2009; http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/WangBlei2009b.pdf and
http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/WangBlei2009c.pdf) if you're
really committed to this model.

Matt

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] problem with implementing Spike and Slab prior for logistic regression
parts:
Right! If you're willing to compromise on "absolute" sparsity and will
be satisfied with a model that only pushes the betas _close_ to zero,
then you can use all sorts of simple models. One of the simplest is
y {0,1 } <--- observed variable
gamma[m] ~ gamma(0.2, 0.2) // selector variable

w[m] ~ Normal(mu[m],sigma[m]) // coefficient
beta[m] = gamma[m]*w[m]
y[n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(x[n] * beta));

The gamma(0.2, 0.2) prior puts about half of its mass below 0.1, so a
priori this model is saying that you expect many of the betas to be
quite small. (Although none of them will be precisely 0.)

Matt

parts: Don't get me started on these spike and slab models.

http://ftp.stat.duke.edu/WorkingPapers/08-31.pdf 

On Sun, Sep 23, 2012 at 3:48 PM, Matt Hoffman <mdho...@cs.princeton.edu> wrote:
Hi Kayhan,

No, people often have reasonable success with Gibbs samplers. Usually
the results are no worse than those obtained using variational
inference (although, as usual when comparing MCMC and variational
approaches, Gibbs may take longer). However, it seems as though these
samplers work poorly when it's not possible to integrate out either
the continuous or the discrete parameters, since there are such strong
posterior dependencies between them. For a (non-conjugate) logistic
regression, integrating out the regression coefficients isn't an
option, but you might be able to adapt the approach of Wang&Blei
(2009; http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/WangBlei2009b.pdf and
http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~blei/papers/WangBlei2009c.pdf) if you're
really committed to this model.

Matt
